title: How to Build a Multilingual Website That Actually Works
excerpt: Most multilingual websites are broken in subtle ways: wrong language served to the right user, duplicate content penalties, language switchers buried in footers. Here's how to build one that doesn't have these problems.

blocks.text: If your business operates across more than one country or language market, at some point you'll need a website that works in multiple languages. What you might not expect is how many ways there are to get this wrong.

A multilingual website isn't just translated pages. It's a site that serves the right language to the right visitor, avoids SEO penalties from duplicate content, and provides a consistent experience regardless of which language a visitor uses. Most multilingual sites fall short on at least one of these.
Here's a practical guide to getting all three right — from URL structure to translation quality to the things most agencies don't warn you about.
Do You Actually Need a Multilingual Site?
Before investing in multilingual infrastructure, ask a simple question: are you losing real revenue because of the language barrier?

Strong signals that you do: your analytics show significant organic traffic from non-primary-language countries, you're already receiving enquiries in other languages, or your direct competitors in target markets run local-language sites.

If you're targeting one country and your customers all speak the same language, multilingual infrastructure adds cost and complexity without a clear return. A single, well-optimised site in your primary language will outperform a hastily translated multilingual one.
URL Structure: The Foundation
How you structure your URLs has consequences for SEO, user experience, and how easy the site is to manage. There are four approaches:

rows: Most businesses — consolidates authority, easy to manage
Large organisations with separate teams per market
Strongest local signal — highest cost and complexity
Avoid — search engines handle it poorly

blocks.text: For most businesses, subdirectory is the right choice. It keeps all your domain authority in one place, is straightforward to implement, and Google handles it reliably. Country domains give the strongest geographic signal but require managing separate domains, separate analytics, and in some cases separate hosting.
hreflang: The Most Commonly Misconfigured Part

hreflang is an HTML attribute that tells search engines which language version of a page to show to which user. Without it, Google might show your German page to French visitors, or rank the wrong language version in the wrong country.

The rules are strict: every language version must reference all other language versions, including itself, in a complete and consistent set. A single broken reference in the chain and Google ignores the whole set.

Common mistakes: forgetting the x-default tag, using relative instead of absolute URLs, omitting a language version from the list. Tools like Screaming Frog or Ahrefs can audit your hreflang implementation. If you've never checked yours, check it — misconfigurations are extremely common even on sites built by agencies.
Translation Quality: Three Levels
There are three tiers of translation quality, and the difference between them is larger than most businesses expect.
Machine translation

Fast and effectively free. Adequate for internal tools, support documentation, or low-stakes informational content. Not adequate for a website that's supposed to persuade people to hire you. Machine translation makes subtle grammatical errors native speakers catch immediately, uses overly literal phrasing, and misses industry-specific terminology.
Professional human translation

A qualified translator produces accurate, grammatically correct output. Better than machine translation, but it may still sound slightly foreign — technically correct, but not how a local business would actually write it. Tone and persuasive punch can get lost in the process.
Native-market copywriting

A native speaker who understands marketing and your specific industry. This is what you want for pages that need to convert. The copy feels written for that market, not translated into it. Idioms, examples, pricing references, and calls to action that work in English often need adapting for German, French, or Dutch audiences — not just word-for-word translation.
Language Detection: Suggest, Don't Force

Automatic language detection based on browser settings or IP address is well-intentioned but frequently annoying. A German-speaking person living in Spain, a bilingual user who uses their browser in English, an expat who wants to read in their native language — all will get the wrong automatic selection.
Best practice: detect and suggest, don't force. Show a non-intrusive banner offering to switch languages. Let users choose. Store their preference so they don't have to re-select it on every visit.
Also put the language switcher somewhere visible — top navigation, accessible on mobile. The number of multilingual sites that bury the language switcher in the footer is striking.
SEO: Keyword Research Doesn't Translate

The search terms your German customers use to find you are not a direct translation of your English keywords. Different languages have different search habits, different levels of competition, and different intent signals.

Each language version of your site needs its own keyword strategy built from search data in that language. This is more work than translating keywords from English, but it's the difference between a multilingual site that ranks organically and one that doesn't.

If you're targeting the German market specifically, note that German search volumes are generally lower than English equivalents — but the competition is also lower, and German buyers tend to research more thoroughly before purchasing.
Content Maintenance: The Ongoing Cost

A multilingual site multiplies your content maintenance burden. Every new page you add needs to be translated. Every update to existing content needs to be reflected across all language versions. If you publish a blog at any frequency, you're looking at ongoing translation costs.

This is where your content architecture matters. A site built with structured content — where pages are composed of translatable content blocks — makes managing multilingual content significantly easier than a site where text is embedded directly in page templates.
What It Costs

rows: Adding multilingual support to existing Next.js site
Ongoing blog translation per post (per language)

blocks.text: A 20-page site built with 3 language versions and native-quality content typically runs €8,000–€18,000 for the complete project including design, development, and content. Adding languages later to a well-architected site is considerably cheaper than rebuilding.
How webvise Approaches Multilingual

Every site we build is multilingual-ready from the start. The webvise.io site itself runs in 7 languages — German, English, French, Spanish, Dutch, Polish, and Italian — served from subdirectory URLs with correct hreflang throughout.

We use a JSON-based content architecture that makes adding new languages or updating translations a structured process rather than a code change. New blog posts go live in all 7 locales simultaneously.
